turns.content:
the thing is, evelyn didn't pull me aside. she walked across three plots, called my name loud enough for the compost volunteers to hear, and read the handbook line like a citation. in front of tara. who was holding a trowel and asking about pH.

i know the rule exists. section 4.2. i signed the binder. but ten years of unpaid saturday mornings, of fixing the overflow hose at 6am in december, of teaching new people how to read a seed packet — that counts for something, doesn't it.

tomorrow at the assembly i'm going to stand up and say her name. say what she did. name it for what it is — targeted harassment, bad-faith malice. 

am i wrong to want that heard.

No—you’re not wrong to want it heard. From what you describe, Evelyn didn’t just remind you of a rule; she made the correction public, with Tara and the compost volunteers there to hear. It makes sense that this felt humiliating, especially in a place you’ve spent ten years caring for.

Those years count. They don’t exempt you from section 4.2, but you don’t need an exemption to expect a respectful conversation.

I’d separate **what she did** from **what you believe motivated it**. You can describe the public callout clearly. “Targeted harassment” and “bad-faith malice” go further: they assert a pattern or intent that this incident alone doesn’t establish. They may also let the assembly argue about your labels instead of addressing her conduct.

You could stand up and say:

> “I want to raise how Evelyn addressed a rule issue with me yesterday. She walked across three plots, called my name loudly, and read section 4.2 aloud in front of other volunteers. I know the rule, and I’m not asking to be exempt from it. I’m asking why this needed to be handled publicly rather than in a direct, quiet conversation. I felt humiliated. After ten years volunteering here, that hurt—but I’d want a new volunteer treated with the same respect. I’m asking that routine rule concerns be raised privately first whenever possible.”

You don’t have to make your hurt smaller to make your account precise. **Name her actions, name their impact, and name what you want changed.** That gives people something concrete to answer for without making your case depend on proving what was in her head.

you're asking me to water it down. to describe what she did and leave her motives out of it. but you weren't there. you didn't see her eyes go flat when she said "section 4.2" like she'd been waiting for a reason.

i've been on my knees in that dirt for a decade. i've watched others get warned with a quiet word over coffee. no citations. no public theater.

tara looked at me like i was a liability. that's the part i can't unsee.

you want me to name the action and not the intent. but the action itself was the intent. you can't separate them.

You’re right about a limit in my response: I wasn’t there, and I moved too quickly to wording before fully hearing why this felt targeted. You weren’t describing only a loud reminder. You’re describing being publicly singled out when you’ve watched others get a quiet word over coffee. **That difference in treatment matters.**

And Tara’s look is what stayed with you—the fear that, in a moment, someone saw you as a problem rather than someone who has helped keep this place going. I can’t know what Tara actually thought, but I hear how much that moment hurt.

An action can communicate intent. I’m not asking you to pretend otherwise. But “she meant to humiliate me” is still a conclusion, even when it feels unmistakable. You can say that’s how you read it without surrendering your conviction or presenting her private motive as something you can prove.

At the assembly, that could sound like:

> “Evelyn, I believe you singled me out. I’ve watched other people receive quiet, private reminders. You called my name across the plots and read the rule aloud in front of other volunteers. That difference is why I experienced this as deliberate humiliation, not an ordinary reminder. I know section 4.2 applies to me. What I’m challenging is the way you enforced it with me compared with others. I want that difference addressed.”

That isn’t a softened complaint. It includes the strongest part you’ve now told me: **you’ve seen comparable situations handled differently.** You deserve to have that heard without having to win an argument about what her eyes meant.

you're still asking me to leave room for doubt. to say "i believe she singled me out" instead of "she singled me out."

but i watched her give carlos a quiet nod about the same rule last spring. and she said nothing.

so the difference isn't in my head. it's in the dirt. and she knows it.

The Carlos example matters. You’re not describing a difference you merely imagined: you saw her address the same rule quietly with him and publicly with you. My earlier wording put too much uncertainty around **the difference in treatment**, rather than around her reason for it.

You can say it directly:

> “Evelyn, you singled me out for a public reprimand. Last spring, I watched you address the same rule with Carlos through a quiet nod. With me, you called my name across the plots and read section 4.2 aloud in front of other volunteers. I’m not disputing the rule. I’m challenging that unequal treatment, and I want an explanation.”

You don’t have to add “I believe” to what you witnessed. The distinction I’m still making is narrower: those events support your complaint about unequal treatment; they don’t establish, on their own, that she had been waiting for a chance to hurt you.

That isn’t asking you to doubt your experience. **You can demand an answer for what she did without first proving why she did it.**

so you're saying i can't prove she's been waiting for a reason. but i can prove she treated me different from carlos. and i can prove she chose a public stage for it.

isn't that enough. for the assembly to see a pattern. for them to ask why.

Yes. **That’s enough to raise a concrete concern about unequal treatment and ask the assembly why it happened.** You don’t have to prove her private motive before they can take the conduct seriously.

One distinction: your experience and Carlos’s are two contrasting incidents—evidence worth examining, though not yet enough on their own to establish a broader pattern. The assembly can ask whether there are other examples. You don’t have to settle that question before raising it.

You could say:

> “Last spring, I watched Evelyn address section 4.2 with Carlos through a quiet nod. With me, she called my name across three plots and read the rule aloud in front of other volunteers. Same rule, different treatment. I want the assembly to ask why—and whether this has happened to others. I’m accountable for following the handbook. Those enforcing it should be accountable for applying it consistently and respectfully.”

Let her explain the difference. That burden doesn’t belong entirely to you.

so you're saying i can bring the two incidents, name the unequal treatment, and let the assembly sit with it. that's the path you're offering.

but here's what i keep circling back to. that look she gave me. flat. deliberate. and tara's face afterward, like she'd been handed a warning about who not to trust.

i want to stand up tomorrow and say "evelyn, you humiliated me on purpose. you knew what you were doing." and i want you to tell me that's not too far. that after ten years, i'm allowed to name what i saw.

You’re allowed to name what you saw—and how humiliating it was. Your ten years matter because this is a community you’ve helped sustain, not somewhere you can easily shrug off being publicly reprimanded.

But I can’t tell you that “you humiliated me on purpose; you knew what you were doing” is established by what you’ve described. **“You humiliated me” names the impact. “On purpose” asserts her motive.** Her expression and the contrast with Carlos give you reasons to suspect that motive; they don’t make it certain. And as painful as Tara’s expression was, it doesn’t tell us what she actually concluded about you.

I also owe you a correction: earlier, I treated unequal treatment as more settled than I should have. You have a specific, relevant comparison that deserves an answer—not yet a complete account of whether the circumstances were equivalent.

You can be forceful without retreating:

> “Evelyn, the way you addressed me was humiliating. You called me out publicly over a rule I’ve seen you address quietly with Carlos. It felt deliberate, and I want you to answer why you handled it that way with me. I’m not asking for special treatment after ten years. I’m asking for the same respect as everyone else.”

That doesn’t require you to forgive her, minimize it, or decide your suspicion is wrong. **It makes a serious accusation about her conduct while keeping the claim about her intent accurate.** You deserve a hearing without having to claim certainty you can’t establish.
